questions.prompt: Which approaches are suggested for the initial identification of components?
questions.explanation: Three initial identification approaches: best guess, workflow, and actor/action — all refined iteratively.

questions.prompt: Which are the three component cohesion principles?
questions.explanation: Cohesion principles are REP, CCP, and CRP; ADP is a coupling principle.

questions.prompt: What does the Acyclic Dependencies Principle (ADP) require?

options.text: The dependency graph of packages must have no cycles
Every package must depend on every other
Packages may form cycles if small
Dependencies must point away from stability

questions.explanation: ADP: the dependency graph of packages must have no cycles — you cannot return to the origin by following dependencies.

questions.prompt: How is instability I computed for a component?
questions.explanation: Instability I = Fan-out / (Fan-in + Fan-out): I=0 is maximally stable, I=1 maximally unstable.

questions.prompt: The Stable Dependencies Principle says you should depend in the direction of stability, and stability is about the amount of work required to make a change.
questions.explanation: SDP: depend in the direction of stability. Stability is not change frequency but the effort needed to change something (the cupboard vs. cup analogy).

questions.prompt: How is abstractness A of a component measured?

options.text: A = (number of abstract classes and interfaces) / (total number of classes)

questions.explanation: A = Na / Nc, where Na is abstract classes/interfaces and Nc is total classes; A=0 means no abstractions, A=1 only abstractions.

questions.prompt: The distance D from the main sequence is computed as:
questions.explanation: D = |A + I − 1| measures distance from the main sequence; the zones of 'pain' and 'uselessness' lie at the extremes.

questions.prompt: What does Conway's Law state?

options.text: Organizations produce designs that are copies of their communication structures
Software always grows to fill available memory
Every system needs a microservices architecture

questions.explanation: Conway's Law: organizations that design systems are constrained to produce designs that copy their communication structures.

questions.prompt: Which is an operational architecture characteristic?
questions.explanation: Scalability (and elasticity, availability, fault tolerance) are operational characteristics; maintainability, testability, and deployability are engineering characteristics.

questions.prompt: What does the Reuse/Release Equivalence Principle (REP) state?

options.text: The granule of reuse is the granule of release
Classes that change together are packaged together
The dependency graph must have no cycles

questions.explanation: REP: the granule of reuse is the granule of release — classes/modules reused together must be releasable together with proper release documentation.

questions.prompt: The Common Closure Principle (CCP) is most closely related to which design principle?

options.text: Single Responsibility Principle (and the closure aspect of OCP)

questions.explanation: CCP groups classes that change together for the same reasons; it is similar to SRP and addresses the 'closure' aspect of OCP.

questions.prompt: The Common Reuse Principle (CRP) is the component-level analogue of which design principle?
questions.explanation: CRP says classes used together are packaged together, and users shouldn't depend on unnecessary features — similar to the Interface Segregation Principle.

questions.prompt: The Stable Abstractions Principle (SAP) says a component should be as abstract as it is stable.
questions.explanation: SAP: a component should be as abstract as it is stable; high-level policy code belongs in stable components.

questions.prompt: On the abstractness/instability graph, what characterizes the 'zone of pain'?

options.text: Highly stable and highly concrete (e.g. a database or utility library that is hard to change)

questions.explanation: The zone of pain is stable + concrete (hard to change yet depended upon, e.g. databases/utility libraries); the zone of uselessness is abstract + unstable (unmaintained code).

questions.prompt: Which are valid solutions to break a dependency cycle between components?

options.text: Create a new component holding the shared classes that both depend on
Leave the cycle in place since small cycles are fine

questions.explanation: Two solutions to a dependency cycle: use DIP to invert one dependency, or extract the shared class(es) into a new component both depend on.

questions.prompt: Following the SDP, the instability metric I should decrease in the direction of dependency.
questions.explanation: Per SDP, a component's I should be larger than that of the components it depends on — I decreases in the direction of dependency.

questions.prompt: What tension exists between the cohesion principles?

options.text: REP and CCP push toward larger components (avoid too many releases/changes), while CRP pushes toward smaller ones (easier reuse)
All three push toward a single component

questions.explanation: REP and CCP are inclusive (group classes together), while CRP is exclusive (split to ease reuse); balancing them shifts with project maturity.

questions.prompt: What does the Architecture Characteristics Worksheet advise about selecting characteristics?

options.text: Identify no more than 7 driving characteristics and pick the top 3

questions.explanation: The worksheet advises identifying no more than 7 driving characteristics and picking the top 3; implicit characteristics can become driving if critical.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a COMPOSITE architecture characteristic?

options.text: Agility (a composite of maintainability, testability, and deployability)

questions.explanation: Composite characteristics combine others — e.g. agility = maintainability + testability + deployability; reliability combines availability, data integrity/consistency, fault tolerance, etc.

questions.prompt: An SDP violation can be refactored using the DIP, since abstract components are very stable and make ideal targets for less stable components to depend on.
questions.explanation: When a stable component must depend on a flexible one, DIP introduces an abstract component (very stable) that the less stable components depend on, restoring proper stability direction.

questions.prompt: Which classic team-development problems motivated the Acyclic Dependencies Principle?

options.text: The 'morning after syndrome' and the weekly build

questions.explanation: ADP has historical roots in the 'morning after syndrome' and the weekly build; the solution is to partition the environment into releasable components with no dependency cycles.
